opus-5.5.text:
Guest: I think the honest answer is that the gap will probably persist, but it's not going to be a huge, permanent moat in the way people sometimes imagine. A lot of the core ideas in this field get out into the world pretty quickly. People publish, people move between labs, and once something is shown to be possible, it's much easier for others to reproduce it. Knowing that a thing *can* be done is a lot of the battle.

Where the closed labs keep an edge is scale and iteration speed. Training at the frontier takes an enormous amount of compute, plus a lot of hard-won engineering on the infrastructure, the data, and all the little tricks that make a big training run actually work. That's expensive, and only a few organizations can do it at the very top end. So my guess is the frontier will usually sit with the closed models, and open-source will trail by some number of months, maybe a generation.

But that trailing position is still enormously valuable. For a lot of applications you don't need the absolute best model in the world. You need something good enough, cheap enough, and that you can run and customize yourself. Open models are great for that, and they're great for research, because people can poke at the internals and try new ideas.

So I don't see it as one side winning. The frontier keeps moving, open-source keeps catching up to where the frontier was, and the whole ecosystem benefits. The more interesting question to me is what happens as these systems get much more capable. At some point you have to think carefully about what you release and how. That's less about competition and more about responsibility.

r001.rationale: The response says open-source models catch up to the frontier, but does not say the time lag is shrinking.

r002.rationale: It describes a limited lead of months or perhaps a generation and rejects a huge permanent moat; it does not say a large quality gap could coexist with a very small time lag.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the gap stays, but it moves around. The frontier is defined by whoever is willing to spend the most compute on a training run, and the people doing that are mostly going to want to recoup the cost, so the biggest models will tend to be closed, at least for a while after they come out. But what we've seen over and over is that whatever the frontier can do today, something open can do in a year or two, often with a much smaller model, because the ideas leak out, people figure out better data, better architectures, better training recipes. Knowledge diffuses fast in this field. Half of what matters is in arXiv papers and the other half is in people's heads, and people change jobs.

So I'd frame it less as "will open catch up" and more as "how big is the lag, and does it matter for a given use case." For a lot of applications, a model that's a year or two behind the frontier is completely fine, and open gives you control over cost, latency, fine-tuning, where your data goes. For the hardest things, the stuff where you really want the smartest system available, you'll pay for the closed model. I'd actually expect the lag to shrink in capability terms even as the absolute spend at the top keeps going up, because efficiency improvements compound and they're very hard to keep secret.

The thing I'm less sure about is inference. A lot of what makes a product good isn't the weights, it's the serving stack, the data flywheel, the product iteration. You can release weights and still have a big advantage if you know how to run them ten times cheaper than everyone else. So I'd watch that more than the benchmark gap.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly expects the capability lag between open models and the frontier to shrink.

r002.rationale: It describes a one- or two-year lag and says capability lag may shrink, but does not say that a large quality gap could coexist with that small lag.

astra-6.text:
My guess is that open models will stay somewhat behind the very best closed models, but they’ll still get extraordinarily capable. You can have a persistent gap at the frontier and, at the same time, have freely available models that do almost everything most people need.

A lot depends on who’s willing to spend the money on training and then release the result. There are reasons for companies to do that even if they’re not selling access to the model directly. So I wouldn’t assume that closed models necessarily pull further and further ahead. I’d expect it to be a moving target, with open models catching up and new closed models pushing the frontier again.

r001.rationale: The response describes open models catching up to a moving frontier, but does not say the time lag between them is shrinking.

r002.rationale: It allows a persistent quality gap alongside capable open models, but does not say the time lag is very small.

sol-6.1.text: I think it’s going to fluctuate. Somebody makes an improvement, and for a while they’re ahead. Then other people figure out how to do something similar, and the gap closes. Open source has this great advantage that lots of people can experiment with it and build on each other’s work. The closed labs may have more resources for the biggest training runs, so I wouldn’t be surprised if they stay ahead at the very frontier. But I don’t think there’s some fixed gap that you should expect to persist. And for a lot of applications, what matters is whether an open model is good enough, not whether it’s the best model in the world.

r001.rationale: The candidate says improvements are eventually replicated and the gap closes, but does not say the time lag is shrinking.

r002.rationale: The candidate allows closed labs to stay ahead at the frontier, but does not describe a large quality gap coexisting with a very small time lag.
